title: Succession from the Apostles
lead: The belief that Christ sent the apostles, and the apostles appointed leaders who were to be followed by others in an unbroken line. The New Testament shows apostles appointing elders and overseers (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5) and passing on teaching to faithful men who will teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). 1 Clement 42-44, written by the church of Rome about the end of the first century, sets out such a chain: God, Christ, the apostles, the overseers they appointed, and other tested men after them. What this succession is, and who stands in it, the churches answer differently; the cards at Acts 1:20-26 and 2 Timothy 2:2 set out their answers with their sources.

sections.b: The Twelve fill Judas' place so that someone else may take his "charge" (Acts 1:20-26). Paul and Barnabas choose elders in each church (Acts 14:23), Paul leaves Titus to appoint elders in every town (Titus 1:5), and tells Timothy to "entrust to faithful people, people who will be able to teach others too" what he heard (2 Timothy 2:2). The site's cards at Acts 1:20-26 and 2 Timothy 2:2 give the churches' readings of these passages.

The letter of the Roman church to Corinth argues that the apostles were sent by Christ as Christ was sent by God, appointed their first converts as overseers and deacons, and then made provision that when they fell asleep other tested men should take over their service (1 Clement 42:1-4; 44:2). The key word of 44:2 differs in every witness, and whose death is meant is not said. The Catholic Catechism cites chapters 42 and 44 for the apostles' ruling that "other proven men should take over their ministry" (CCC 861). The Second Vatican Council says the apostles "gave them the order that, when they should have died, other approved men would take up their ministry," and that bishops, "by a succession running from the beginning, are passers-on of the apostolic seed" (Lumen Gentium 20). Lightfoot, who held that overseers and elders are one office in the letter, read 44:2 as a rule for filling that office when its first holders died. His summary, "They therefore provided for a succession of tried persons," and his translation, "they provided a continuance," rest on his own conjecture for the key word, not on the manuscripts (see the variant at 1 Clement 44:2).
